enforcement_note: Nothing can mechanically decide whether a class has one responsibility - that is a judgement about intent, not a property of the syntax tree. A linter can measure method count and fan-out; it cannot tell a cohesive five-method class from an incoherent one. The real mechanism is the agent answering these questions honestly during Phase 2 and recording what it found, plus the user reading the diff.
condition: Reviewing or writing object-oriented or module-structured code.
rule: Audit new and changed code against the SOLID principles, as questions rather than prescriptions.
ai_action: Work through the checklist against the code you just wrote. Report the answers, including the ones that pass - a checklist that only ever surfaces problems gets read as noise. Where a principle is knowingly traded away, say which and why rather than staying silent.

questions: Does this class or module have one reason to change? Name it. If naming it needs an 'and', that is two.
Would a change to persistence, to presentation, and to business rules all touch this same file?
Can the next variation be added without editing this code, or does every new case mean another branch here?
Is the extension point a real seam, or an abstraction invented for a second case that has not arrived?
Can every subtype stand in for its base without the caller knowing which it got?
Does any override narrow what the base promised - throwing where the base returned, or ignoring an argument the base honoured?
Does any implementer leave methods empty or raise NotImplemented? That is the interface asking for too much.
Would splitting this interface leave each caller depending only on what it actually calls?
Does the policy depend on the detail, or the detail on the policy?
Can this be tested without the database, the network, or the clock? If not, the dependency is concrete where it should be injected.

anti_pattern: Do not turn these into prescriptions. 'Use an interface for every service' produces indirection nobody needed; 'does this have one reason to change?' produces a look at the code. The question survives contact with a codebase it was not written for. The prescription does not.

provenance.source: agent-generated; SOLID as stated by Robert C. Martin, Agile Software Development: Principles, Patterns, and Practices (2002)
provenance.basis: Harvested as the first 05-domains checklist under .ai/GROWTH.md. Phrased as review questions per the checklist-not-prescription rule.
